paragraphs: Friend, the first part of this passage is heavy. Gedaliah promises the commanders that "it will be well with you," and then the passage says Ishmael struck him down (2 Kings 25:24-25). Here's what I take from it: a promise from a person can be cut short, and people run when that happens (2 Kings 25:26). I think that's worth saying plainly instead of rushing past it.

Then the passage jumps to Babylon, in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, and the tone changes (2 Kings 25:27). Evil-merodach "released King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison" and "spoke kindly to Jehoiachin" (2 Kings 25:27-28). The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess, but it does end the chapter with a kindness instead of the killing at Mizpah. Jehoiachin eats at the king's table "for the rest of his life" (2 Kings 25:29).

So here's what I want you to carry out of my bakery, baker. A promise from a person can break, but a small kindness is still a real kindness, and it's worth noticing when one shows up. I can't tell you your hard season will flip like Jehoiachin's did, because this passage doesn't promise that. I can tell you I got called out of the back of a junk drawer once and never saw it coming, so I keep my ovens warm and my eyes open.
